psych_HU_2014.explanation: Shaping is the operant-conditioning procedure of reinforcing successive approximations until the final desired response is achieved.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 11) Alem had a rough day, and his son's homemaking was not helping him relax. Not wanting himself to scolding, he told his son in a serious manner that he was very tired and would like the boy to play quietly for an hour. This approach worked. For Alem, the change in his son's behavior was (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: The son’s quiet behavior removed the aversive noise and avoided further scolding, illustrating negative reinforcement of the quiet-play response.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 12) In ________ learning, a new behavior is learned but is not shown until appropriate reinforcement is presented. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Latent learning is the acquisition of knowledge that remains hidden until a suitable incentive or reinforcement appears.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 13) You studied the history of Middle East two years ago. You now find yourself unable to recall what you learned which is also caused by non-use. This situation can be best explained by (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Decay theory attributes forgetting to the gradual fading of memory traces over time when they are not used or rehearsed.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 14) Your psychology professor tells you, when we lack something, we are motivated to get it." Which approach to motivation does your professor subscribe to? (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Drive-reduction theory holds that physiological deficits create drives that motivate the organism to reduce the deficit and restore balance.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 15) I help an elderly person cross the street because doing a good deed makes me feel good. What type of motivation is at work here? (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Helping because it produces internal feelings of satisfaction is intrinsic motivation; no external reward is required.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 16) Pavlov is famous for his work in: (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Ivan Pavlov discovered classical conditioning through his experiments on salivary reflexes in dogs.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 17) In punishment which is applied to modify a behaviour: (2014)

options.text: A. severe punishments are less effective than mild ones.
B. when punishment is inconsistent the behaviour becomes extinct.
C. consistency is about when punishment follows after the behaviour
D. less intense punishments can be effective if they are applied immediately and consistently.

psych_HU_2014.explanation: Effective punishment depends more on immediacy and consistency than on intensity; mild but consistently and immediately applied punishment can suppress behavior.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 18) If we reinforce the desired response every time it occurs, we are using: (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Continuous reinforcement delivers a reinforcer after every occurrence of the target response and produces rapid acquisition.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 19) Taking away a child's toys after she has hit her brother (to stop her hitting him again!) is an example of: (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Negative punishment removes a desirable stimulus contingent on an undesired behavior, thereby decreasing the future probability of that behavior.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 20) According to the behavioural learning theory perspective, ______ plays no role in learning. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Behavioral theories emphasize environmental experience (nurture) and largely discount innate factors (nature) as determinants of learning.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 21) Giving a student extra work after they misbehave in class is an example of: (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus following an undesired behavior in order to decrease that behavior.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 22) To train her puppy to roll over, Maji began by rewarding it for simply lying down. The reward continued in each step until it finally rolls over. Maji was using: (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Shaping reinforces successive approximations of the target behavior until the final response is achieved.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 23) Positive reinforcement ______ the likelihood of a behaviour, and negative reinforcement ______ the likelihood of a behaviour. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Both positive reinforcement (adding a desirable stimulus) and negative reinforcement (removing an aversive stimulus) increase the future probability of the behavior they follow.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 24) Banak got sick after eating a peach. Now he feels sick when he looks at peaches, nectarines or plums. This illustrates: (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Stimulus generalization occurs when a conditioned response elicited by one stimulus also occurs to similar stimuli.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 25) A bakery gives customers a free pastry after every 6 pastry purchases. This is an example of what kind of reinforcement schedule? (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: A fixed-ratio schedule delivers reinforcement after a constant number of responses (every sixth purchase).

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 26) Insight learning is a cognitive process whereby (2014)

options.text: A. It depends on conditioning of particular behaviours for its occurrence
B. we solve a problem by focusing only on one aspect of the problem
C. we reorganize our perception of a problem.

psych_HU_2014.explanation: Insight learning involves a sudden reorganization of the perceptual field that yields a solution, rather than gradual trial-and-error or simple conditioning.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 27) An intermittent schedule of reinforcement that reinforces behaviour after an average, but unpredictable, amount of time has passed is called a ______ schedule. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: A variable-interval schedule reinforces the first response after an unpredictable average time interval has elapsed.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 28) Food is to ______ reinforcer as money is to ______ reinforcer. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Food is a primary reinforcer because it satisfies a biological need; money is a secondary reinforcer whose value is learned through association with primary reinforcers.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 29) After being bitten by a big Alsatian dog, Hugo was scared of other big dogs but he was not scared of little dogs like Chihuahuas. This pattern demonstrates: (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Stimulus discrimination is the ability to respond differently to stimuli that differ on relevant dimensions (size of the dog).

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 30) You are online one evening when an advert appears showing your favourite movie star wearing a new brand of sunglasses. The advertiser hopes that your positive feelings toward the movie star will make you want the sunglasses. In this situation, the sunglasses would be the: (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: In classical-conditioning advertising, the previously neutral product becomes a conditioned stimulus by pairing with a positive unconditioned stimulus (the liked celebrity).

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 31) People who have a lot of dental problems often come to dislike even the smell of their dentist's office. The smell represents a(n): (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: The originally neutral office smell becomes a conditioned stimulus after repeated pairing with aversive dental procedures.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 32) Taking away a person's car after they have been caught for exceeding the speed limit would be an example of: (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Removal of a valued possession contingent on the undesired behavior constitutes negative punishment.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 33) Suppose, you are walking down a dark road late at night. You hear footsteps behind you and you begin to tremble, your heart beats faster, and your breathing deepens. You notice these physiological changes, and interpret them as your body's preparation for a fearful situation. You then experience fear. This example belongs to ______ theory. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: The James-Lange theory holds that the experience of emotion follows the perception of bodily arousal; the physiological changes are interpreted as fear.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 34) Assume, you are walking down a dark road late at night. You hear footsteps behind you and you begin to tremble, your heart beats faster, and your breathing deepens. Upon noticing this arousal you realize that it comes from the fact that you are walking down a dark road by yourself. This behavior is dangerous and therefore you feel the emotion of fear. This particular example belongs to ______ theory of emotion. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: The Schachter-Singer (two-factor) theory states that emotion results from physiological arousal plus a cognitive label of the situation that produced the arousal.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 35) Assume, you are walking down a dark road late at night. You hear footsteps behind you and you begin to tremble, your heart beats faster, and your breathing deepens. At the same time as these physiological changes occur you also experience the emotion of fear. This particular example belongs to ______ theory of emotion. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: The Cannon-Bard theory asserts that physiological arousal and the subjective experience of emotion occur simultaneously and independently.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 36) Escaping penalty by paying "Iqqub" fees on time is a best example of (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Paying on time removes or avoids the aversive penalty, thereby negatively reinforcing the timely-payment behavior.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 37) Assume, you are walking down a dark road late at night. You hear footsteps behind you and you think it may be a robber so you begin to tremble, your heart beats faster, and your breathing deepens and at the same time you experience fear. This particular example belongs to ______ theory of emotion. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Lazarus’s cognitive-appraisal theory emphasizes that emotion arises from an immediate cognitive evaluation of the situation that simultaneously generates both arousal and the feeling of fear.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 38) The first step in social learning theory is ______. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Bandura’s observational-learning sequence begins with attention: the observer must first notice and attend to the model’s behavior.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 39) In the categories of long-term memory, the memory about one's own life is ______ memory. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Episodic memory is the long-term store of personally experienced events and autobiographical information.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 40) Mistaking the sound of an ambulance in the city for the sound of police cars and going out from home to escape since he committed a crime the other day is an example of ______. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Stimulus generalization is responding to a stimulus that resembles the original conditioned stimulus.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 41) Continuing playing football betting because of the fact that one has sparingly won some money (previously) by doing so ______. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Partial (intermittent) reinforcement, especially on a variable-ratio schedule, produces persistent behavior even when wins are infrequent.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 42) Aberu and Fikir are University lecturers. They are intimate friends. They usually debate on some issues, such as on meaning or interpretation of democracy, violence against women, and religion. In such debate one tries to persuade the other by listing out the possible reasons. Which one of the following types of long-term memory is most likely to be used in the debate? (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Semantic memory stores general knowledge, concepts, and facts that are drawn upon when constructing logical arguments and definitions.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 43) When an extinguished behaviour suddenly reappears on its own, with no retraining, the process is called ______. (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of a previously extinguished conditioned response after a rest period without further pairing.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 44) Disasa quickly learned how to change a tire. His knowledge remained dormant until the day he got a flat tire and had to change the tire. This illustrates the concept of: (2014)
psych_HU_2014.explanation: Latent learning is knowledge acquired without immediate reinforcement that becomes evident only when a need or incentive arises.

psych_HU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_HU_2014.text: 45) In Bandura's description of modelling a behaviour retention refers to: (2014)

options.text: A. the person must first pay attention to the model.
B. the observer must be able to remember the behaviour that has been observed.
C. the ability to replicate the behaviour that the model has just demonstrated.
D. learners must want to demonstrate what they have learned.

psych_HU_2014.explanation: Retention is the second process in Bandura’s model: the observer must encode and store a mental representation of the observed behavior so that it can later be reproduced.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 1) According t biological perspective, the cause of psychological disorder is a result of inappropriate learning. (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: The biological perspective attributes psychological disorders to organic or physical causes, such as genetic inheritance, biochemical imbalances in the brain, or structural brain abnormalities. Inappropriate learning is the focus of the behavioral perspective.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 2) Retroactive forgetting theorists believe that information learnt previously is powerful to banish the current memory/information. (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Retroactive interference (forgetting) occurs when newly learned information interferes with the recall of previously learned information. The statement describes proactive interference, where older information interferes with the recall of newer information.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 3) The presence of abnormal behavior solely can be sufficient for the diagnosis of psychologica problem. (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Diagnosing a psychological problem requires more than just the presence of abnormal behavior. Clinicians consider a combination of factors, often referred to as the "four D's": deviance, distress, dysfunction (maladaptiveness), and danger to self or others. Context and culture also play a significant role.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 4) According to Carl Rogers, unconditional positive regard is a key to achieve or realize self-actualization. (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Carl Rogers, a humanistic psychologist, believed that receiving unconditional positive regard—being accepted and loved for who you are, without conditions—is essential for developing a healthy self-concept and moving towards self-actualization.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 5) Self actualized persons are realistic, high achievement oriented and have high self confidence. (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: While self-actualized individuals are realistic and self-accepting, they are not typically characterized as "high achievement oriented" in the conventional sense of pursuing external success. Their motivation is intrinsic, focused on personal growth and fulfilling their potential, rather than competitive achievement.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 6) According to psychoanalytic theory of personality our behavior is not freely chosen it is determined by intra-psychic forces. (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Freud's psychoanalytic theory is deterministic, proposing that behavior is largely determined by unconscious forces (the id, ego, and superego) and childhood experiences, rather than by conscious free will.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 7) The emotions we experience daily are obvious to observers and they can affect our social interaction (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Emotions have observable components, such as facial expressions, body language, and tone of voice, which make them communicate to others. These emotional displays play a crucial role in regulating and influencing social interactions.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 8) Ego personality is the first most primitive and pleasure oriented part of personality. (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: In Freud's theory, the **id** is the most primitive part of the personality, present at birth and operating on the pleasure principle. The **ego** develops later and operates on the reality principle, mediating between the demands of the id, the superego, and reality.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 9) Introverts are outgoing and sociable, whereas extraverts are more solitary and dislike being the center of attention. (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: This statement reverses the definitions. Extraverts are characterized by being outgoing, sociable, and energized by social interactions. Introverts are typically more solitary, reserved, and prefer less stimulating environments.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 10) Motivation is always followed by drive and needs. (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: The typical motivational cycle begins with a **need** (a physiological or psychological deficiency), which creates a **drive** (an internal state of tension or arousal). This drive then motivates behavior aimed at satisfying the need.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 1. Refusal to believe one's results when graded "F" (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Denial is a defense mechanism that involves refusing to accept or acknowledge a painful or threatening reality, such as failing a grade.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 2. A person who is fired from his job says "the job was not a good one." (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Rationalization involves creating false but plausible excuses to justify unacceptable behavior or to minimize the impact of a disappointing event, like being fired, in order to protect one's self-esteem.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 3. "I do not ignore him, he ignores me." (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Projection is the defense mechanism of attributing one's own unacceptable thoughts, feelings, or motives to another person.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 4. A person forgets that he was tortured severely (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Repression is the unconscious blocking of unacceptable or traumatic thoughts, feelings, and impulses from conscious memory.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 5. A father shouts at his wife and children after quarrelling with his boss. (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Displacement involves redirecting emotional feelings (often anger or aggression) from their original, threatening target to a safer, substitute target.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 1) According to the humanistic motivation theory of Abraham Maslow, self-actualized people are (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Maslow described self-actualized individuals as having a clear perception of reality, being open to experiences (which can include spiritual or peak experiences), and being spontaneous and unconventional, not bound by rigid social norms.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 2) Mr. Dana is a student of Wolaita Sodo University. He always studies hard because he gets personal satisfaction by studying. His desire to read connects to which of the following? ---- (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Intrinsic motivation refers to performing an activity for its own sake, out of personal interest or for the inherent satisfaction it provides, rather than for some separable consequence like a reward or to avoid punishment.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 3) Which of the following statements aligned with the James-Lang theory of emotion? (2013)

options.text: A. Emotional experiences are dependent upon physiological responses.
B. Emotions are objective responses to experiences in our environment.
C. Emotions are the result of an individual's emotional intelligence
D Emotional experiences are dependent upon physiological responses and how a person interprets those responses.

psych_WSU_2013.explanation: The James-Lange theory of emotion asserts that physiological arousal precedes and causes the experience of emotion. We feel afraid because we tremble, not the other way around. Option D describes the Schachter-Singer two-factor theory.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 4) For the past six months, Julie has been exhausted, hopeless, and unable to enjoy her normal up at work. The most likely diagnosis is (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: The symptoms described—prolonged exhaustion, hopelessness, and anhedonia (inability to experience pleasure)—are classic indicators of a major depressive episode. The duration of six months is well beyond the minimum required for diagnosis.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 5) Since it is stressful for her, Miss. Meron doesn't want to recall the rape since she faced from her father This type of forgetting is more attributed to which of the following forgetting theory? (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Motivated forgetting, a concept closely related to the psychoanalytic idea of repression, suggests that people may unconsciously block out painful, traumatic, or anxiety-provoking memories to protect themselves from psychological distress.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 6) Which one of the following is false about motivation? (2013)

options.text: A. Maslow's hierarchy of needs describes how some of our needs take priority over others.
B. Drive reduction theory focuses on how our inner pushes and external pulls interact.
C. For Maslow, once our higher -level needs are met, we prompted to satisfy our lower-level needs.
D. Arousal theory focuses on finding the right level of stimulation.

psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is organized such that lower-level physiological and safety needs must be met before higher-level needs like esteem and self-actualization become primary motivators. The statement in option C is the reverse of this principle.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 7) In Freud's Personality theory, the ego operates according to the ______ principle (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: In Freud's theory, the ego operates on the reality principle, which seeks to gratify the id's impulses in realistic ways that will bring long-term pleasure rather than pain or destruction. The id operates on the pleasure principle, and the superego on the morality principle.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 8) A perspective that analyses of brain structure and nervous system function as a cause of psychological disorder is (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: The biological perspective focuses on the physical and biological bases of behavior and mental processes, including how genetics, brain structure, and neurochemistry can contribute to psychological disorders.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 9) Kidusan checks light switches, water facets, the stove and looks doors at least three times before going to bed. This scenario describes which of the following anxiety disorders? (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: The behavior described—repetitive checking of items to relieve anxiety—is a classic example of a compulsion, which is a hallmark symptom of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD). The checking is done to prevent a feared event or to reduce distress.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 10) Which one of the following statements is not true about personality? (2013)

options.text: A Personality deals with a collection of independent attributes or characteristics.
B. Personality does not refer to simple mixture of different characteristics.
C. Personality implies the identity of a person.
D. Personality deals with unified characteristics of a person.

psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Personality is defined as an organized and dynamic set of characteristics possessed by a person that uniquely influences their cognitions, motivations, and behaviors. It is not a loose collection of independent traits but an integrated and unified whole.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 11) Mr. Tolosa just switched from using his mobile password to a new one, and he is frustrated because he keeps trying to use the old password to open the mobile. This is an example of (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Proactive interference occurs when previously learned information (the old password) interferes with the ability to recall newly learned information (the new password).

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 12) A disorder that involves displaying one's bodies to impecting ang is (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Exhibitionism is a paraphilic disorder characterized by the urge, fantasy, or act of exposing one's genitals to unsuspecting strangers for sexual gratification. (Note: The text "impecting ang" appears to be a typo for "unsuspecting strangers").

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 13) In which Freud's psycho-sexual stage children get satisfaction by playing with their peers and fo on school activities. (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: The latency stage is a period in Freud's psychoanalytic theory (roughly from age 6 to puberty) during which sexual feelings are dormant. Children's energy is directed towards school, hobbies, and same-sex friendships.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 14) An interviewer asked the graduating class student of WSU about the interesting event/moment that Hirut spent in her university. She said that she loved the crazy day event that she enjoyed with her course mate, which was really wonderful one". Her memory seems (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Episodic memory is a subcategory of declarative memory that stores personal experiences that are tied to specific times and places, such as attending a specific event like "crazy day" at university.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 15) Mr. Dawit was living in Hawassa city, one day he started his journey to Axum to visit his relatives but on the way to Axum at Gonder city the bus he was in fortunately crushed with other bus and experienced accident, after that accident Dawit totally lost his memory and forgot from where he came and where he was going, then he went to Assosa and started living there and took new identity. which kind of Psychological disorder is it? (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Dissociative fugue is a rare disorder characterized by reversible amnesia for personal identity, including the memories, personality, and other identifying characteristics of individuality. The state is usually accompanied by unplanned travel or wandering, and sometimes the establishment of a new identity.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 16) Mr. Motuma loves her husband and children very much. She got a highly paid job very far away from her home town. This may force her to leave her family. Both situations are attractive. She could not decide to choose one. The type of conflict is... (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: An approach-approach conflict occurs when a person must choose between two desirable or attractive goals. In this case, the individual wants to stay with her loving family and also wants to take the highly paid job.

psych_WSU_2013.subject: Psychology
psych_WSU_2013.text: 17) Imote is defining the term 'psychology' exactly as she has learned two years ago. From which long term memory she is extracting this information? (2013)
psych_WSU_2013.explanation: Semantic memory refers to a portion of long-term memory that processes ideas and concepts that are not drawn from personal experience. It includes things that are common knowledge, such as the names of colors, the capitals of countries, and definitions of terms like 'psychology'.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 1. Unlike sensory memory, short term has a very limited storage capacity. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Short-term memory has a limited capacity, often cited as holding about 7 ± 2 items for a short duration (around 20-30 seconds). In contrast, sensory memory has a large capacity but a very brief duration (fraction of a second to a few seconds).

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 2. Super ego refers to the internal representation of morals, values and cultures of the society. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: In Freud's psychoanalytic theory, the superego is the component of personality that is composed of the internalized ideals and moral standards that we acquire from our parents and society. It provides guidelines for making judgments (the conscience) and for future aspirations (the ego ideal).

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 3. Storage is the process of retaining information in memory for later use. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Memory involves three fundamental processes: encoding (getting information into memory), storage (retaining information over time), and retrieval (getting information out of storage). Therefore, storage is correctly defined as the retention of encoded information.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 4. Negative reinforcement decreases the chance that the behavior will occur again. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Reinforcement, by definition, increases the likelihood of a behavior. Negative reinforcement increases behavior by removing or avoiding a negative or aversive stimulus. Punishment is what decreases the likelihood of a behavior.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 5. Memory system that stores information from our visual system is echoic memory. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: The sensory memory register for visual information is called iconic memory. Echoic memory is the sensory memory register for auditory information.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 6. Emotions are feelings of a person that can be expressed by our physical body and actions. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Emotions are complex psychological states that involve three components: a subjective conscious experience (feeling), physiological arousal (bodily response), and behavioral or expressive response (actions, facial expressions).

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 7. Incentives are internal states that push individuals towards a goal. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Incentives are external stimuli (objects or events) that motivate behavior by pulling or attracting an individual towards a goal. Internal states that push an individual are typically referred to as drives or needs.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 8. Extrinsic motivation has a longer lasting effect than intrinsic motivation. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Intrinsic motivation, which comes from within the individual and is driven by interest or enjoyment in the task itself, generally leads to more persistent and long-lasting engagement. Extrinsic motivation, driven by external rewards or avoiding punishment, tends to have a more temporary effect and can sometimes undermine intrinsic motivation.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 9. Freud viewed that people feel competent when their real and ideal self are very close to each other. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: The concept of the real self and ideal self, and the idea that congruence between them leads to competence and well-being, is a central tenet of Carl Rogers' humanistic theory of personality, not Freud's psychoanalytic theory.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 10. Chunking is the process of grouping bits of information into a single unit. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Chunking is a memory strategy that involves organizing or grouping separate bits of information into larger, more meaningful units or 'chunks'. This process helps increase the limited capacity of short-term memory.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 11. A person is unable to remember the painful trauma. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Repression is a defense mechanism in psychoanalytic theory where anxiety-provoking thoughts, feelings, and memories are banished from conscious awareness.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 12. A situation in which you refuse to accept reality. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Denial is a defense mechanism in which a person refuses to acknowledge or accept a painful or threatening reality, acting as if it does not exist.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 13. Shouting at your wife after a quarrel with your boss (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Displacement is a defense mechanism that involves redirecting emotional impulses (usually aggression or sexual impulses) from a threatening or unavailable target to a less threatening or more available one.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 14. Placing your unacceptable impulses on others (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Projection is a defense mechanism where an individual attributes their own unacceptable thoughts, feelings, or motives to another person.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 15. Giving acceptable reasons for inappropriate behaviors (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Rationalization is a defense mechanism where a person creates false but plausible excuses to justify unacceptable behavior or to minimize the impact of a disappointing event.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 16. A tendency to act in a manner opposite to one's true feelings (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Reaction formation is a defense mechanism in which the ego unconsciously switches unacceptable impulses into their opposites. Thus, people may express feelings that are the opposite of their anxiety-arousing unconscious feelings.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 17. A soap factory pays 100 birr for each worker if he/she produces 100 packs of soaps. What kind of reinforcement schedule is this? (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: A fixed-ratio schedule reinforces behavior after a specific number of responses. In this case, the worker is reinforced with payment after the fixed number of 100 packs produced.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 18. Removing something which is pleasant in order to discourage wrong behavior is the best example of: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Punishment is a consequence that decreases the likelihood of a behavior. Negative punishment involves the removal of a pleasant or desirable stimulus to decrease a behavior.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 19. Which one of the following is not a primary reinforcer? (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Primary reinforcers are naturally rewarding because they satisfy basic biological needs (e.g., food, water, sleep). Money is a secondary or conditioned reinforcer because its value is learned through its association with primary reinforcers.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 20. Learning through observation is the basic assumption of _____: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Social learning theory, proposed by Albert Bandura, posits that people learn from one another, primarily through observation, imitation, and modeling.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 21. Which of the following represents the correct order of basic processes of observational learning? (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: According to Bandura's social learning theory, observational learning involves four essential processes in this order: (1) Attention to the model, (2) Retention of what was observed, (3) Production or reproduction of the behavior, and (4) Motivation to perform the behavior.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 22. According to operant conditioning theory, a relatively permanent change in behavior occurs when (2014)

options.text: A. Conditioned stimulus associated with unconditioned stimulus
B. Voluntary response is accompanied by favorable or unfavorable consequences
C. Neutral stimulus acquires all the characteristics of the natural stimulus
D. Involuntary emotional response occurs as result of natural stimulus

psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Operant conditioning is a type of learning where behavior is controlled by consequences. A voluntary response is followed by a reinforcing or punishing consequence, which then influences the future probability of that response. The other options describe classical conditioning.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 23. In order to answer this exam, you need to access stored information for your use. This process is called: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Retrieval is the memory process of getting information out of storage. Taking an exam requires accessing and bringing to mind information that has been previously encoded and stored.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 24. Which one is not a characteristic of working memory? (2014)

options.text: B. Its capacity is very limited
C. Information stored for indefinite periods
D. It is known as working memory

psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Working memory is a system for temporarily storing and managing the information required to carry out complex cognitive tasks. It has a limited capacity and duration. Indefinite storage is a characteristic of long-term memory.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 25. Well-learned materials are permanently stored in: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Long-term memory is the relatively permanent and limitless storehouse of the memory system. Information that is well-learned is consolidated and stored here for long periods.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 26. Suppose that Muse is able to remember the distance between Addis Ababa and Bahir Dar in Kilometers. The type of memory that Muse typically uses is _____ : (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Semantic memory is a type of long-term declarative memory that stores general knowledge, facts, concepts, and meanings that are not tied to specific personal experiences. Knowing a factual distance between two cities is a classic example of semantic memory.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 27. Mr. Yonas is trying to recall his old email address to look over his inbox. But, he couldn't remember it, instead he remembers the recently developed address. This is due to: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Retroactive interference occurs when newly learned information (the recently developed email address) interferes with and impedes the recall of previously learned information (the old email address).

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 28. Which theory of motivation proposes that we are motivated to maintain equilibrium in body and/or interest? (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Drive reduction theory is based on the idea that a physiological need creates an aroused tension state (a drive) that motivates an organism to satisfy the need and restore homeostasis, or a state of internal equilibrium.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 29. Which theory of motivation believes that all individuals are born with innate motivations that are essential for survival? (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Instinct theory suggests that organisms are born with innate, unlearned, and biologically determined patterns of behavior, called instincts, that motivate actions essential for survival.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 30. An individual who is quiet, reserved, shy and unsociable is best described as having: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Introversion is a personality trait characterized by a focus on internal feelings rather than on external sources of stimulation. Introverts tend to be quiet, reserved, and less sociable than extraverts.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 31. What is the source of forgetting according to decay theory of forgetting? (2014)

options.text: A. Interference of similar items of information with one another
B. Spread of new information entering memory over old information
C. Memory traces fade because of the passage of time
D. Conscious blocking of those memories that are too threatening

psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Decay theory proposes that forgetting occurs because memory traces (engrams) fade or disintegrate over time if they are not accessed or rehearsed. The simple passage of time is the cause of forgetting in this view.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 32. Which statement is not true about personality? (2014)

options.text: B. Personality is stable over time
D. Personality is stable across situations

psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Personality refers to an individual's unique and relatively stable patterns of thinking, feeling, and behaving. While culture can influence personality traits, the particular combination of traits that makes up an individual's personality is considered unique to them, not a set of shared characteristics.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 33. The part of personality structure that is guided by reality principle is: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: In Freud's psychoanalytic theory, the ego is the component of personality that operates on the reality principle. It seeks to satisfy the id's impulses in realistic and socially acceptable ways, balancing the demands of the id, the superego, and reality.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 34. A personality disorder characterized by a pattern of disregard for the rights of others is: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Antisocial personality disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of disregard for, and violation of, the rights of others. This can include behaviors such as deceitfulness, impulsivity, irritability, and lack of remorse.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 35. Which symptom is not common among patients with major depressive disorder? (2014)

options.text: A. Excessive involvement in pleasurable activities
B. Minimum or no involvement in pleasurable activities

psych_DMU_2014.explanation: A core symptom of major depressive disorder is anhedonia, which is a loss of interest or pleasure in activities that were once enjoyed. Excessive involvement in pleasurable activities is typically associated with manic episodes in bipolar disorder, not depression.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 36. A personality disorder characterized by an exaggerated self-image and need for admiration is: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Narcissistic personality disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of grandiosity (in fantasy or behavior), a constant need for admiration, and a lack of empathy for others.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 37. An anxiety disorder known for its symptoms of fear of public or marketplaces is: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Agoraphobia is an anxiety disorder characterized by a fear of being in situations where escape might be difficult or help wouldn't be available if things go wrong. This often leads to the avoidance of public places like markets, crowds, or open spaces.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 38. One of the following is a situation in which an individual is facing two unattractive goals. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: An avoidance-avoidance conflict occurs when an individual is forced to choose between two equally undesirable or unattractive alternatives.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 39. A criterion of psychological disorder known for its deviation from cultural standards and norms is: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: In the context of defining psychological disorders, abnormality (specifically, deviance) refers to behavior, thoughts, or emotions that differ significantly from a society's accepted norms and cultural standards.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 40. Which of the following therapeutic models is the best to treat depression? (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Cognitive therapy, particularly Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT), is widely recognized as one of the most effective evidence-based treatments for depression. It focuses on identifying and changing negative thought patterns and beliefs that contribute to the depressive state.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 41. The view that bacterial infection or physical disease is the cause of psychological disorders is advocated by: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: The biological perspective (also known as the medical model) views psychological disorders as having physical causes, such as genetics, biochemical imbalances, brain abnormalities, or infections.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 42. Which theory of emotion supports the belief that the experience of an emotion occurs simultaneously with bodily arousal? (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: The Cannon-Bard theory of emotion proposes that an emotion-provoking stimulus triggers physiological arousal and the subjective experience of emotion simultaneously and independently. One does not cause the other.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 43. Yibelital, whose hobby is visiting historical places, tells his friend about a holiday celebrated in Aberha Mariam even though he has never seen it before. Yibelital's information is stored in: (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Semantic memory is the part of long-term memory responsible for storing general knowledge, facts, and concepts that are not tied to specific personal experiences. Since Yibelital has not personally experienced the celebration, his knowledge about it is semantic.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 44. According to Maslow's needs hierarchy, what motives will be most important in a person's behavior? (2014)

options.text: C. Secondary drives that are easily attend

psych_DMU_2014.explanation: According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, needs are arranged in a hierarchy of prepotency. Lower-level needs (physiological, safety) must be met before higher-level needs (belongingness, esteem, self-actualization) can become primary motivators. Therefore, at any given time, behavior is motivated by the lowest unsatisfied need in the hierarchy.

psych_DMU_2014.subject: Psychology
psych_DMU_2014.text: 45. Mention the three components of emotion. (2014)
psych_DMU_2014.answer: The three components of emotion are: 1) Physiological arousal (bodily responses), 2) Expressive behaviors (outward signs like facial expressions), and 3) Conscious experience (subjective feelings and thoughts).
psych_DMU_2014.explanation: Emotions are complex psychological states that involve these three distinct but interrelated components, which work together to define the emotional experience.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 1. Searching for safe circumstances, stability and protection belongs to the need for love and affection.
psych_WU.explanation: According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, searching for safe circumstances, stability, and protection belongs to the 'safety needs' level, which is distinct from and lower than the 'love and belonging' needs.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 2. A need to climb a tree and afraid of falling simultaneously is an example of App Approach conflict.
psych_WU.explanation: An approach-avoidance conflict occurs when a single goal or activity has both attractive (climbing the tree) and repelling (fear of falling) aspects.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 3. All theories of emotion agree that thoughts always precede emotions.
psych_WU.explanation: Not all theories agree. For example, the James-Lange theory posits that physiological arousal precedes the experience of emotion, and the Zajonc-LeDoux theory suggests some emotional responses occur instantly, before cognitive appraisal.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 4. According to trait theory of personality, the ultimate goal of personality growth is self-actualization.
psych_WU.explanation: Self-actualization is the ultimate goal of personality growth according to humanistic theories of personality (e.g., Maslow, Rogers), not trait theories, which focus on identifying and measuring personality characteristics.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 5. When a decision one is going to make is so important the conflict of motives and frustra also become greater.
psych_WU.explanation: Decisions of greater importance typically involve more significant consequences and stronger competing motives, leading to increased internal conflict and potential frustration.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 1. Pattern of instability in personal relationships
psych_WU.explanation: Borderline Personality Disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affects, along with marked impulsivity.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 2. Pattern of grandiosity and exaggerated self-worth
psych_WU.explanation: Narcissistic Personality Disorder is defined by a pervasive pattern of grandiosity (in fantasy or behavior), need for admiration, and lack of empathy.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 3. Pattern of feelings of social inadequacies, low self-esteem
psych_WU.explanation: Avoidant Personality Disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 4. Pattern of excessive emotional behavior and attention seeking
psych_WU.explanation: Histrionic Personality Disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of excessive emotionality and attention-seeking behavior.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 5. Pattern of discomfort in close relationships
psych_WU.explanation: Schizotypal Personality Disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of social and interpersonal deficits marked by acute discomfort with, and reduced capacity for, close relationships, as well as by cognitive or perceptual distortions and eccentricities of behavior.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 6. Pattern of distrust and suspiciousness
psych_WU.explanation: Paranoid Personality Disorder is characterized by a pervasive distrust and suspiciousness of others such that their motives are interpreted as malevolent.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 7. Pattern of disregard for the rights of others
psych_WU.explanation: Antisocial Personality Disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 8. Pattern of detachment from social norms
psych_WU.explanation: While the phrasing is imperfect, this description best fits Schizoid Personality Disorder among the remaining options. Schizoid PD is characterized by a pervasive pattern of detachment from social relationships and a restricted range of expression of emotions in interpersonal settings, which can manifest as indifference to social norms and conventions.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 1. A psychologist who emphasizes the stimuli that provoke observed responses and ten avoid the concept of mental processes was most likely trained in _____ tradition.
psych_WU.explanation: Behaviorism is the school of psychology that focuses on observable behaviors and the environmental stimuli that elicit them, explicitly rejecting the study of internal mental processes which they deemed unobservable and unscientific.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 2. A group of farmers attempts to discourage foxes from attacking their sheep by plac substance on the wool of the sheep that makes foxes violently ill if they eat it. quickly, the foxes avoid the sheep entirely. In this scenario, what are the UCS, CS CR, respectively?

options.text: A. The substance, the sheep's wool, aversion to the sheep
B. The Foxes, the sheep's wool, aversion to sheep
C. Aversion to sheep, the substance, the sheep's wool
D. The sheep's wool, the substance, aversion to sheep

psych_WU.explanation: In this classical conditioning example, the substance that causes illness is the Unconditioned Stimulus (UCS) because it naturally triggers the Unconditioned Response (UCR) of becoming ill. The sheep's wool is initially a neutral stimulus that becomes the Conditioned Stimulus (CS) after being paired with the substance. The aversion to the sheep is the Conditioned Response (CR) elicited by the sheep's wool alone.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 3. The same farmers discover that now not only will the foxes not attack the treated s but also they will not attack nearby sheep. This is an example of:
psych_WU.explanation: Stimulus generalization occurs when a Conditioned Response (CR) is elicited by stimuli that are similar, but not identical, to the original Conditioned Stimulus (CS). In this case, the foxes' aversion (CR) generalized from the treated sheep (CS) to other similar nearby sheep.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 4. Ato Girma, an English teacher, gives quizzes to his students every marking period. is an example of:

options.text: A. Variable interval schedule of reinforcement
B. Fixed interval schedule of reinforcement
C. Variable ratio schedule of reinforcement
D. Fixed ratio schedule of reinforcement

psych_WU.explanation: A fixed interval schedule of reinforcement provides reinforcement (the quiz/grade) for the first response made after a specific, fixed period of time has elapsed. Giving quizzes at the end of every marking period is a classic example of a fixed interval schedule.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 5. In what manner would Ivan Pavlov have conducted extinction trials on his classic conditioned dogs?

options.text: A. Reinforcing the behavior he wished to extinguish
B. Repeatedly presenting dogs with the food and the bell at the same time
C. Repeatedly presenting the CS (bell) without pairing it with the US (food)
D. Immediately giving the dogs food (UCS) after the bell (CS) rings

psych_WU.explanation: Extinction in classical conditioning occurs when the Conditioned Stimulus (CS) is repeatedly presented alone, without being paired with the Unconditioned Stimulus (US). This process gradually weakens and eventually eliminates the Conditioned Response (CR).

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 6. Which of the following is true of classical conditioning?
psych_WU.explanation: In classical conditioning, the Unconditioned Stimulus (UCS) is a stimulus that naturally and automatically triggers an Unconditioned Response (UCR) without any prior learning.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 7. A coach who tries to get a player to come closer and closer to a particular movement needed in the sport is probably using:
psych_WU.explanation: Shaping is an operant conditioning procedure in which reinforcers guide behavior toward closer and closer approximations of the desired behavior. The coach is reinforcing successive approximations of the correct movement.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 8. A rat being reinforced on a fixed ratio of 15 (FR= 15) is being reinforced

options.text: B. After a US presented every 15 seconds
C. For a response after each 15 second period
D. For a certain number of responses

psych_WU.explanation: A fixed ratio (FR) schedule of reinforcement delivers reinforcement after a specified, fixed number of responses. An FR=15 schedule means the rat is reinforced after every 15th response.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 9. If the removal of a stimulus strengthens or maintains a response, it probably is correct to say that
psych_WU.explanation: Negative reinforcement occurs when a behavior is strengthened or maintained by the removal or avoidance of an aversive stimulus. The term 'negative' here means something is taken away.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 10. What is one major difference between operant conditioning (OC) and classical conditioning (CC)?

options.text: A. OC takes place before the response, while CC takes place after the response
B. OC is learned by association, while CC is learned by reinforcement
C. OC takes place as a result of some voluntary action, while CC takes place without choice
D. CC is part of social cognitive learning, while OC is not

psych_WU.explanation: A key difference is that classical conditioning involves associating an involuntary, reflexive response with a stimulus, while operant conditioning involves associating a voluntary behavior with a consequence.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 11. Which of the following examples best illustrates episodic memory?

options.text: A. Knowing that Christopher Columbus sailed in 1492
B. Teaching someone how to play tennis
D. Remembering that you got a bicycle for your 12th birthday

psych_WU.explanation: Episodic memory is the memory of autobiographical events (times, places, associated emotions, and other contextual who, what, when, where, why knowledge) that can be explicitly stated. Remembering a specific personal event like getting a bicycle on a specific birthday is a clear example of episodic memory.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 12. When asked why she fears spiders, Sophia is unable to explain her fears, where they came from, or how she got them. This is an example of:

options.text: A. Semantic memory, which helps us avoid painful memories
B. Procedural memory, which holds memories that we are not aware of
C. Echoic memory, which holds memories we cannot retrieve
D. Episodic memory, which has knowledge of specific personal memories

psych_WU.explanation: Phobias and other emotional responses often involve implicit memory, which is unconscious. While procedural memory typically refers to motor skills, the broader category of implicit memory includes emotional conditioning where the original association is not consciously remembered. Option B is the best fit among the choices, as it correctly identifies the unconscious nature of this type of memory.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 13. Suppose you are absorbed in reading a novel and a friend asks you a question. You reading and ask, "What did you say?" As soon as the words leave your mouth, you realize you can recall your friend's exact words. What is the reason for your ability to play back these words?
psych_WU.explanation: Echoic memory is the sensory memory register specific to auditory information (sounds). It holds a brief "echo" of what was just heard for a few seconds, allowing you to process and recall it even if your attention was momentarily elsewhere.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 14. Value and respect for all of a person's behavior with no condition would be classified by Rogers as:-
psych_WU.explanation: Unconditional positive regard is a concept developed by humanistic psychologist Carl Rogers, referring to the basic acceptance and support of a person regardless of what they say or do.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 15. Which type of memory is also referred to as working memory?
psych_WU.explanation: Working memory is a more contemporary term for short-term memory, emphasizing its role as an active processing system that temporarily holds and manipulates information required for complex cognitive tasks.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 25. While waiting for his car to be fixed, a man was suddenly overcome by an intense fear which he had never experienced before. His heart beat raced so fast he felt as if he was having a heart attack. He may be showing the symptoms of
psych_WU.explanation: A panic disorder is characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks—sudden periods of intense fear or discomfort that include physical symptoms like palpitations, pounding heart, and a feeling of unreality or being detached from oneself.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 26. In reading a restaurant menu, trying to choose between two very tasty entrees illustrates.
psych_WU.explanation: An approach-approach conflict occurs when a person must choose between two or more desirable alternatives.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 27. An individual who shows extremes of mood and activity level is most likely to be diagnosed as having
psych_WU.explanation: Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition that causes extreme mood swings that include emotional highs (mania or hypomania) and lows (depression), affecting activity levels, energy, and the ability to function.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 28. According to the drive-reduction theory, the drive to eat can come from

options.text: B. An attempt to reduce hunger
C. A state of tension caused by innate drives

psych_WU.explanation: Drive-reduction theory proposes that physiological needs (like the need for food) create an uncomfortable state of tension or arousal (a drive, like hunger) that motivates an organism to satisfy the need and reduce the tension, returning the body to homeostasis.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 29. The concept that emotions resulted from perceived bodily changes was the key to:-
psych_WU.explanation: The James-Lange theory of emotion suggests that emotions occur as a result of physiological reactions to events. In other words, we experience an emotion because we perceive our bodily changes.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 30. According to the Cannon-Bard theory, which two factors are simultaneously activated by environmental stimuli?
psych_WU.explanation: The Cannon-Bard theory states that an emotion-provoking event leads simultaneously to both an emotional experience (feeling) and physiological reactions (arousal). These two occur at the same time and independently of each other.

psych_WU.subject: Psychology
psych_WU.text: 1. List and explain at least five Freud's Ego defense mechanisms. (10 pts)
psych_WU.answer: 1. Repression: The unconscious blocking of unacceptable thoughts, feelings, and impulses. The key is that it happens unconsciously. 2. Denial: The refusal to accept reality or fact, acting as if a painful event, thought, or feeling did not exist. It is considered one of the most primitive defense mechanisms. 3. Projection: The misattribution of a person's undesired thoughts, feelings, or impulses onto another person who does not have those thoughts, feelings, or impulses. 4. Displacement: The redirecting of thoughts, feelings, and impulses directed at one person or object, but taken out upon another person or object. People often use displacement when they cannot express their feelings in a safe manner to the person they are directed at. 5. Rationalization: Putting something into a different light or offering a different explanation for one's perceptions or behaviors in the face of a changing reality. 6. Sublimation: The channeling of unacceptable impulses, thoughts, and emotions into more acceptable ones. It is often considered a mature defense mechanism. 7. Regression: The reversion to an earlier stage of development in the face of unacceptable thoughts or impulses. 8. Reaction Formation: The converting of unwanted or dangerous thoughts, feelings, or impulses into their opposites.
psych_WU.explanation: Freud's ego defense mechanisms are unconscious psychological strategies used by the ego to protect itself from anxiety arising from unacceptable thoughts or feelings. The question asks for a list and explanation of at least five of these mechanisms. The provided answer lists and defines eight common examples.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 1. Self-concept is having a clear perception of your personality, including strengths, weaknesses, thoughts, beliefs, motivation, and emotions.
psych_GU.explanation: Self-awareness is having a clear perception of your personality, whereas self-concept is the overarching idea or image one has of who they are. The provided statement specifically defines self-awareness, making it false.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 2. Resilience is the process of adapting well in the face of adversity, trauma, tragedy, threats or significant sources of stress.
psych_GU.explanation: Resilience is defined in psychology as the psychological quality that allows individuals to adapt effectively and bounce back from significant adversity, trauma, tragedy, or profound stress.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 3. Extraversion can best be described as a person's willingness to try new things and be open to new experiences.
psych_GU.explanation: A person's willingness to try new things and be open to new experiences defines the personality trait of Openness to experience. Extraversion is characterized by outgoing, energetic, and highly sociable behavior.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 4. According to Freud, early experience has more impact on our development of personality than later experience.
psych_GU.explanation: Sigmund Freud's psychoanalytic theory emphasizes that adult personality is fundamentally shaped by childhood experiences, particularly how one navigates early psychosexual stages and underlying conflicts.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 5. Freud ego defense mechanisms are not solution by themselves rather they are escaping mechanisms.
psych_GU.explanation: Freudian defense mechanisms are unconscious psychological strategies employed by the ego to protect against anxiety and internal conflict. They act as temporary coping or escaping mechanisms to manage distress rather than solving the root psychological issues.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 6. Primary drives are those that are learned through experience or conditioning, such as the need for money, social approval.
psych_GU.explanation: Primary drives are innate, unlearned biological needs necessary for survival, such as hunger and thirst. Drives for money or social approval are acquired through experience and are termed secondary drives.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 7. As to the James-Lange theory, emotions are created by awareness of specific patterns of peripheral (autonomic) responses.
psych_GU.explanation: The James-Lange theory posits that emotional experience is the direct result of recognizing and interpreting specific physiological (autonomic) reactions to an external stimulus.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 8. Emotion refers to factors that influence the initiation, direction, intensity, and persistence of behavior.
psych_GU.explanation: The factors that initiate, direct, intensify, and persist behavior define motivation. Emotion, while related, refers specifically to a complex subjective experience encompassing physiological arousal, cognitive appraisal, and behavioral expression.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 9. Self-control is achieved by refraining from actions we like and instead performing actions we prefer not to do as a means of achieving a long-term goal.
psych_GU.explanation: Self-control involves the regulation of impulses and the delay of immediate gratification, which often means enduring short-term discomfort or denying short-term pleasure in service of a more valuable long-term goal.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 10. Self-confidence refers to an individual's overall self-evaluation.
psych_GU.explanation: An individual's overall self-evaluation and sense of global self-worth is called self-esteem. Self-confidence refers to a person's trust in their own abilities, capacities, and judgments regarding specific tasks or situations.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 1. Physiological need (Part II. Match level of Maslow humanstics need listed under column "A" with their respective major features presented under column "B")

options.text: A. Need for protection from danger or external aggressors.
B. Need for the things that will make him/her enjoy considerable influence from others
C. Need to achieve success and avoid failure
D. Needs include the desire of people to pursue admire beautiful things
F. Aspiration of man to establish a cordial relationship with others

psych_GU.explanation: Physiological needs are the biological requirements and most basic requirements for human survival, matching the description of 'Survival needs of man'.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 2. Safety need (Part II. Match level of Maslow humanstics need listed under column "A" with their respective major features presented under column "B")

options.text: A. Need for protection from danger or external aggressors.
B. Need for the things that will make him/her enjoy considerable influence from others
C. Need to achieve success and avoid failure
D. Needs include the desire of people to pursue admire beautiful things
F. Aspiration of man to establish a cordial relationship with others

psych_GU.explanation: Safety needs emerge once physiological needs are met, manifesting as a drive for protection, security, stability, and freedom from fear or external danger.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 3. Love and belongingness need (Part II. Match level of Maslow humanstics need listed under column "A" with their respective major features presented under column "B")

options.text: A. Need for protection from danger or external aggressors.
B. Need for the things that will make him/her enjoy considerable influence from others
C. Need to achieve success and avoid failure
D. Needs include the desire of people to pursue admire beautiful things
F. Aspiration of man to establish a cordial relationship with others

psych_GU.explanation: Love and belongingness needs involve interpersonal relationships, affiliating with others, and establishing cordial, affectionate connections within groups.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 4. Esteem need (Part II. Match level of Maslow humanstics need listed under column "A" with their respective major features presented under column "B")

options.text: A. Need for protection from danger or external aggressors.
B. Need for the things that will make him/her enjoy considerable influence from others
C. Need to achieve success and avoid failure
D. Needs include the desire of people to pursue admire beautiful things
F. Aspiration of man to establish a cordial relationship with others

psych_GU.explanation: Esteem needs encompass both internal factors like mastery and external factors like prestige, status, and recognition, which correlates with desiring influence from others.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 5. Actualization need (Part II. Match level of Maslow humanstics need listed under column "A" with their respective major features presented under column "B")

options.text: A. Need for protection from danger or external aggressors.
B. Need for the things that will make him/her enjoy considerable influence from others
C. Need to achieve success and avoid failure
D. Needs include the desire of people to pursue admire beautiful things
F. Aspiration of man to establish a cordial relationship with others

psych_GU.explanation: In this specific curriculum framework, self-actualization encompasses expansive growth motivations, which heavily overlap with aesthetic needs—the pursuit and appreciation of beauty.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 1. Abeba always feels like she is never included in group activities or social events. She has become depressed and lonely. According to Maslow, which category of needs has not been fulfilled by her?
psych_GU.explanation: Feelings of loneliness, depression, and being excluded from social events directly point to an unmet need for social relationships, affiliation, and affection, which Maslow categorized as Love and belongingness needs.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 2. A self-actualized person is:

options.text: A. Lacking autonomy but has many friends
B. Is common in the population
D. A person who focuses on problems outside of themselves

psych_GU.explanation: According to Maslow, self-actualized individuals are relatively rare, highly autonomous, have frequent peak experiences, and tend to be problem-centered (focusing on goals and causes outside themselves) rather than self-centered.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 3. Tigist likes to attend the movies, but she is concerned with how expensive ticket prices are getting and the cost of concessions. She wants to have fun, but she also knows that she needs to save money for college. Which type of motivational conflict is Tigist experiencing?
psych_GU.explanation: An approach-avoidance conflict occurs when an individual is drawn to a single goal that has both positive (having fun) and negative (costing money) characteristics simultaneously.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 4. Unlike her co-workers, Hana were motivated by challenge, personal satisfaction, and by doing interesting work; most of her coworkers were just in it for the money. Hana was motivated by
psych_GU.explanation: Intrinsic motivation involves engaging in a behavior because it is personally rewarding and fulfills internal drives such as personal satisfaction and intellectual challenge, rather than relying on external rewards like money.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 5. Instead of taking out his anger on his wife, john break his saxophone. This is example of what defense mechanism?
psych_GU.explanation: Displacement is a defense mechanism wherein a person shifts unacceptable emotional impulses (like anger) from a primary, often threatening target (his wife) to a secondary, less threatening target or object (his saxophone).

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 6. Anna husband dies, and she continues to set a place for him at the dinner table. This is an example of
psych_GU.explanation: Denial involves an outright refusal to accept reality or fact, acting as if a painful event, thought, or feeling did not exist. Setting a place for a deceased spouse represents a denial of their death.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 7. Un faithful husband might suspect his wife to have affair with others
psych_GU.explanation: Projection is a defense mechanism where individuals attribute their own unacceptable thoughts, feelings, or motives to another person. Here, the husband attributes his own infidelity onto his wife.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 8. A fired student might say, I fired from the school because there is no sufficient reading material, teachers do not teach well and some teacher hate me.
psych_GU.explanation: Rationalization entails creating false but plausible excuses to justify unacceptable behaviors, outcomes, or failures. By blaming external factors rather than their own performance, the student is rationalizing the expulsion.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 9. If a person comes across a snarling dog while taking a walk, the physical arousal is accompanied by the thought that must be fear. For which theory does it related?

options.text: A. Schechter-Singer and Cognitive Arousal Theory
C. James Lang Theory of Emotion

psych_GU.explanation: The Schachter-Singer two-factor theory states that emotion is based on two factors: physiological arousal and a cognitive label. The presence of physical arousal paired explicitly with the cognitive interpretation ('the thought that must be fear') defines this theory.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 10. Avoidance-avoidance conflict occurs when

options.text: A. An individual is faced with decisions to pursue something that has only disadvantages
B. An individual is faced with decisions to pursue something that has only advantages
C. An individual is faced with a decision to pursue or avoid something that has advantages and disadvantages
D. A group of people are faced with a decision to pursue or avoid something that has advantages and disadvantages

psych_GU.explanation: Avoidance-avoidance conflict describes a situation where an individual must choose between two highly undesirable or negative alternatives. Option A describes being forced to choose among options that possess only negative characteristics.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 11. From trait personality dimension, a willingness to try new things and be open to new experiences is
psych_GU.explanation: In the Big Five personality model, Openness to experience involves characteristics such as imagination, intellectual curiosity, and a willingness to try new things.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 12. Self-control mean

options.text: A. The ability to regulate your urges.
B. The ability to tell yourself what to do rather than someone else telling you.
C. The ability to understand who you really are.
D. The ability to stick to something.

psych_GU.explanation: Self-control fundamentally means having the psychological capacity to override or regulate one's immediate impulses, emotions, and urges in order to behave appropriately or achieve long-term goals.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 13. Self-awareness mean

options.text: A. The ability to understand who you really are.
B. The ability to stick to something
C. The ability to interact with others in a positive way.
D. The ability to feel what others feel.

psych_GU.explanation: Self-awareness is defined as having a clear and objective perception of one's own personality traits, beliefs, emotions, and underlying motives, effectively encompassing an understanding of who you really are.

psych_GU.subject: Psychology
psych_GU.text: 14. What is the first step of decision making process?
